### Random-field simulations

To quantitatively evaluate the structure-function mapping hypothesis, we set out to simulate a set of grid cells in three-dimensional anatomical space. The grid phases associated with these grid cells follow the correlation structure suggested by Gu et al., 2018, and Heys et al., 2014. Our aim is to quantify the clustering of grid phases for a realistically sized fMRI voxel given this correlation structure.

We use a three-dimensional representation of a voxel with a volume of 3 × 3 × 3 mm3. Within this voxel, we define a grating of 2003 potential grid cells that are equally spaced in the voxel, with a distance between neighboring cells of 15 μm along the axes of the grating. To generate a set of random but spatially correlated grid phases on this area, we first define two random unit vectors in the complex plane, $Z_{1}$ and $Z_{2}$, for each of the 2003 potential grid cells in the voxel; angles of the unit vectors are thus drawn from a uniform distribution on the interval $[0,2\pi)$. $Z_{1}$ and $Z_{2}$ are further resolved into their real and imaginary components $Re(Z_{i})$ and $Im(Z_{i})$, respectively, where $i\in{1,2}$. To generate correlations between grid phases, we then convolve the two resulting gratings of 2003 components separately with either a Gaussian kernel (Figure 4K) or a grid kernel (Figure 4O) to yield the convolved components $Re(Z^_{i})$ and $Im(Z^_{i})$. The grid phases can be obtained by first calculating the angles of the new set of complex numbers and normalizing the result by $2\pi$:

$$
x^_{off}=\frac{arg(Z^_{1})}{2\pi}y^_{off}=\frac{arg(Z^_{2})}{2\pi}.
$$

We note that $x^_{off}$ and $y^_{off}$ are defined on the interval $[0,1)$ and correspond to the grid phases of a single grid cell mapped to the unit square. Transforming the result to the unit rhombus yields the grid phases $x_{off}$ and $y_{off}$ in the $x$ and $y$ direction respectively:

$$
x_{off}=x^_{off}+\frac{y^_{off}}{2}y_{off}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}y^_{off}
$$

To find the average pairwise grid phase distances as a function of the pairwise anatomical distances, 108 pairs of grid cells are sampled randomly from the uniform distribution defined on the discrete space of grating cell positions. The Euclidean distance in anatomical space between the two grid cells in each pair is calculated and sorted into 50 bins of equal width on the interval [10, 500] μm. Then, for each pair of grid cells, $n_{1}$ and $n_{2}$, eight copies of the grid phase $(x_{off,2},y_{off,2})$ of the second cell $n_{2}$ are made, which are offset from the initial position of the grid phase such that they are positioned at the same phase within unit rhombi laid end-to-end on a 3 × 3 grid. The minimum distance between the grid phase of the cell $n_{1}$ and the grid phase of each of the copies of the cell $n_{2}$ is taken as the pairwise phase distance. Finally, the pairwise distance between grid phase offsets per distance bin is obtained by taking the mean over all grid cell pairs whose Euclidean distance in anatomical space falls into the corresponding bin (Figure 4H, L, and P).

To estimate the clustering concentration parameter $κ_{s}$ in Figure 4, the phases $x^_{off}$ and $y^_{off}$ are mapped to a circular distribution by multiplying them with $2\pi$. The sets of grid phases ${2\pix^_{off}^{i}|i\in{1,2,...,N}}$ and ${2\piy^_{off}^{i}|i\in{1,2,...,N}}$ are then each separately fit to a one-dimensional von Mises distribution to obtain a clustering concentration parameter for each axis. The final value of $κ_{s}$ is taken as the average of these two values.

### Parameter estimation

The hexasymmetry values of the tested hypotheses depend on the respective parameters. We investigate two scenarios for each hypothesis: an ‘ideal’ set of parameters that results in a large (basically maximal) hexasymmetry value and a ‘realistic’ set of parameters that we try to derive from experimental data. All sets of parameters are summarized in Table 1, i.e., the symbols are introduced and defined, and parameter values and units are stated. We comment here on the ‘realistic’ sets of parameters and how we derived them.

#### Conjunctive grid by HD hypothesis

For the ‘realistic’ value of $\sigma_{c}=3^{∘}$, we use the 95% confidence interval of 12.4° from the third row of the table in the Supplementary Figure 5b of Doeller et al., 2010, and translate this value to a Gaussian standard deviation, assuming a 95% confidence interval of $4\sigma_{c}$.

For the ‘realistic’ value of $κ_{c}=4$, we refer to the Supplementary Figure 3 of Doeller et al., 2010. Visually, the tuning curves usually cover between one sixth and one third of the circle. Stronger HD tuning contributes the most to the resulting hexasymmetry, so we choose a value of $κ_{c}=4$, which corresponds to a tuning width of roughly one sixth of the circle. For further discussion on $κ_{c}$, see also Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

The ‘realistic’ value of $p_{c}=1/3$ was chosen based on the values reported by Sargolini et al., 2006, and Boccara et al., 2010. In our simulations, we observed that the hexasymmetry shows a linear dependence on the fraction of conjunctive cells up to a noise floor (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).

#### Repetition suppression hypothesis

To obtain ‘realistic’ parameter values, we simply divide the ‘ideal’ ones by two, which results in a ‘realistic’ adaptation time constant $\tau_{r}=1.5$ s and a ‘realistic’ adaptation weight $w_{r}=0.5$. ‘Ideal’ parameter values attenuate the firing rate by ≈20% (Figure 3A, with 24% when running aligned with the grid axes and 18% when running misaligned to the grid axes). ‘Realistic’ parameter values attenuate firing rates by ≈16% (for a dependence of hexasymmetry on the two parameters, see Figure 3B). Such a decrease has a similar order of magnitude as the attenuation of 5% of firing rates in Reber et al., 2023 (their Figure 2B, right). The value of the ‘realistic’ time constant is also comparable to the time scales found in two electrophysiological studies: first, Giocomo and Hasselmo, 2008, showed that the time constant in the slow component of the hyperpolarization-activated current ($I_{h}$) in the ventral mEC is 2–3 s (their Figure 2F). Second, Magistretti and Alonso, 1999, found a second-long inactivation of a persistent sodium current in EC layer II cells.

#### Structure-function mapping hypothesis

The ‘realistic’ value of the concentration parameter for clustering, $κ_{s}=0.1$, is derived from the random-field simulations in Figure 4G–S and a comparison to results in Gu et al., 2018, and Heys et al., 2014. Figure 4G in Gu et al., 2018, shows for grid cells in the rat mEC the relationship between their pairwise physical distance and their pairwise phase distance. Similarly, for grid cells in the mouse mEC, Heys et al., 2014, in their Figure 4B show the correlation of (one-dimensional) grid firing maps as a function of anatomical pairwise distance between grid cells. Together, these data serve as evidence for more similar grid cell firing for anatomically close grid cells (distance <100 μm)—with decreasing similarity for increasing anatomical distance. In our random-field simulations (Figure 4), we mimic these experimental results by choosing the width of a spatial correlation kernel accordingly (Figure 4K, Gaussian kernel with standard deviation: 30 μm). Consequently, in the simulations, the initial rise of phase distance as a function of anatomical distance (Figure 4L) reflects the experimental curves. In Gu et al.’s Figure 4G there is a slight increase in grid-firing similarity (decrease of phase distance) for anatomical distances of approximately 300 μm. In our simulations, we reflect such a non-monotonous behavior by introducing a grid-like correlation kernel (Figure 4O) with a grid spacing of 300 μm. Applying this grid-like correlation kernel to the random field in Figure 4G results in a phase-distance curve with a slight dip around 300 μm (Figure 4P), just like in the experimental curves in Gu et al., 2018. For both cases, the Gaussian kernel and the grid-like kernel, we find that the resulting phase clustering for an anatomical voxel of realistic size is quite low, i.e., $κ_{s}$ is well below 0.1 (Figure 4M and Q). As it poses an upper bound for the realistic values of $κ_{s}$, we use 0.1 as an estimate of the ‘realistic’ value for $κ_{s}$ in our further simulations. For the central phase of the cluster, we always use (without loss of generality) the origin: $\mu_{s}=(0,0)$.

### Implementation of previously used metrics

We applied three previously used metrics to our framework: the GLM method by Doeller et al., 2010; the GLM method with binning by Kunz et al., 2015, the circular-linear correlation method by Maidenbaum et al., 2018; Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

In brief, in the GLM method (e.g. used in Doeller et al., 2010), the hexasymmetry is found in two steps: the orientation of the hexadirectional modulation is first estimated on the first half of the data by using the regressors $\beta_{1}cos⁡(6\theta_{t})$ and $\beta_{2}sin⁡(6\theta_{t})$ on the time-discrete fMRI activity (Equation 9), with $\theta_{t}$ being the movement direction of the subject in time step $t$. The amplitude of the signal is then estimated on the second half of the data using the single regressor $\betacos⁡[6(\theta_{t}−ϕ)]$, where $ϕ=arctan⁡(\beta_{2}/\beta_{1})/6$. The hexasymmetry is then evaluated as $H=\beta/2$.

The GLM method with binning (e.g. used in Kunz et al., 2015) uses the same procedure as the GLM method for estimating the grid orientation in the first half of the data, but the amplitude is estimated differently on the second half by a regressor that has a value 1 if $\theta_{t}$ is aligned with a peak of the hexadirectional modulation (aligned if $|\theta_{t}−ϕ|%60^{∘}<15^{∘}$, % modulo operator) and a value of −1 if $\theta_{t}$ is misaligned. The hexasymmetry is then calculated from the amplitude in the same way as the GLM method.

The circular-linear correlation method (e.g. used in Maidenbaum et al., 2018) is similar to the GLM method in that it uses the regressors $\beta_{1}cos⁡(6\theta_{t})$ and $\beta_{2}sin⁡(6\theta_{t})$ on the time-discrete mean activity, but instead of using $\beta_{1}$ and $\beta_{2}$ to estimate the orientation of the hexadirectional modulation, the beta values are directly used to estimate the hexasymmetry using the relation $H=\sqrt{\beta_{1}^{2}+\beta_{2}^{2}}/2$.

Regarding the statistical evaluation, each method evaluates the size of the neural hexasymmetry differently. Specifically, the new method developed in our manuscript compares the neural hexasymmetry to path hexasymmetry to test whether neural hexasymmetry is significantly above path hexasymmetry. For the two GLM methods, we compare the hexasymmetry to zero (using the Mann-Whitney U test) to establish significance. Hexasymmetry values can be negative in these approaches, allowing the statistical comparison against 0. Negative values occur when the estimated grid orientation from the first data half does not match the grid orientation from the second data half. Regarding the statistical evaluation of the circular-linear correlation method, we calculated a z-score by comparing each empirical observation of the hexasymmetry to hexasymmetries from a set of surrogate distributions (as in Maidenbaum et al., 2018). We then calculate a p-value by comparing the distribution of z-scores versus zero using a Mann-Whitney U test. We use the z-scores instead of the hexasymmetry for the circular-linear correlation method to match the procedure used in Maidenbaum et al., 2018. We obtained the surrogate distributions by circularly shifting the vector of movement directions relative to the time-dependent vector of firing rates. For random walks, the vector is shifted by a random number drawn from a uniform distribution defined with the same length as the number of time points in the vector of movement directions. For the star-like walks and piecewise linear walks, the shift is a random integer multiplied by the number of time points in a linear segment. Circularly shifting the vector of movement directions scrambles the correlations between movement direction and neural activity while preserving their temporal structure.

### Tuning widths and the large-κ approximation

The numerical values of our tuning width of HD modulated cells should not be directly compared to the numbers reported by Sargolini et al., 2006, with values in the range of 55° because Sargolini et al., 2006 reported the tuning widths as the angular standard deviation $\sigma$ of the mean vector of HD-dependent firing rates whereas we derive the tuning width from the large-$κ_{c}$ approximation of a von Mises distribution: $\sigma=1/\sqrt{κ_{c}}$. This simple approximation is reasonably good only for large enough $κ_{c}$ (or small enough $\sigma$), and 55° is already beyond the range where the approximation is reasonable (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).

To examine the range of values where the large-$κ_{c}$ approximation holds, we can compare it to the angular standard deviation expressed as $\sigma=\sqrt{−2ln⁡[I_{1}(κ_{c})/I_{0}(κ_{c})]}$, where $I_{n}(κ_{c})$ is the modified Bessel function of the first kind of order ‘n’. This equation is valid for all values of the concentration parameter $κ_{c}$. The results of this comparison are summarized in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B. In brief, the large-$κ_{c}$ approximation closely matches the angular standard deviation for $κ_{c}>4$, which corresponds to $\sigma<29^{∘}$. The angular standard deviation $\sigma=55^{∘}$ reported by Sargolini et al., 2006 corresponds to a concentration parameter $κ_{c}$ of about 1.7 and (in our large-$κ_{c}$ approximation) to a tuning width $1/\sqrt{κ_{c}}=44^{∘}$ (upward triangle in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and C).

### Numerical simulations

All simulations were implemented in Python 3.10 using the packages NumPy, SciPy, Numba, and JobLib. Matplotlib was used for plotting. Inkscape was used for the final adjustment to the figures.

Essential revisions (for the authors):

1) Strengthen the link between the simulations presented here and the known biophysical properties of rodent entorhinal grid cells. Revise the ranges used in the analyses in comparison with those reported in the literature (see details for each scenario below) and provide a graphical representation of the values in each case. Provide an idea of how values of H are related to results obtained with other methods in previous experimental studies.

2) Extend the study to null-hypothesis scenarios, such as the standard grid cell model or head-direction clustering that is independent of grid cell firing.

Reviewer #1 (Recommendations for the authors):

Suggestions for improvement to the authors:

Is there quantitative evidence independent of the Doeller (2010) paper that head direction selectivity is clustered along the grid axes?

Similarly, is there quantitative evidence independent of the Heys (2014) and Gu (2018) papers for the clustering of spatial phases?

Can effective firing rate adaptation parameters be somehow gauged from studies of the real biophysical properties of grid cells, as in the early Giocomo and Hasselmo studies? Obtaining "realistic" parameters just by dividing by 2 ideal parameters seems a bit arbitrary.

Congratulations on the nice study, especially the valuable analytical components!

With regards to the structure-function hypothesis, and following the comments above, the authors should also state how the 'realistic' values of the clustering parameter that they refer to in Sections 2.2.3 and 2.3 were derived from data presented by Gu et al. (2018), and what those parameter values are

Reviewer #3 (Recommendations for the authors):

1. Could the null hypothesis of trajectory-dependent hexasymmetry be mapped out more clearly? For example:

- It's implicit that a 'standard' grid cell model wouldn't generate hexadirectional modulation. It could help the reader to make this clear early in the introduction.

- The Methods and Supplemental Data illustrate the possibility that hexadirectional modulation could arise simply from the trajectory followed – called path hexasymmetry here. The very nice modelling approach used provides an opportunity to quantify the size of this effect relative to effects in previous human studies and to verify that previous attempts to mitigate this through binning were successful. Adding this analysis would be a valuable control for the interpretation of human data.

- For the conjunctive grid model, is there anything special about the neurons being grid cells? In other words, would head direction cells with similar tuning profiles generate the same hexadirectional modulation? I expect they would but clarity here would be helpful for future mechanistic work.

2. It could also help the reader to illustrate the head direction parameters for each simulation, alongside the results. E.g. With plots of the head direction tunings for the models presented.

claims.claim: Hexadirectional modulation is not clearly supported by a bias of grid cells toward a particular phase offset.
claims.source: Here, we use numerical simulations and analytical calculations to suggest that this hexadirectional modulation is best explained by head-direction tuning aligned to the grid axes, whereas it is not clearly supported by a bias of grid cells toward a particular phase offset.
claims.evidence: This is supported by simulations showing that realistic clustering parameters result in substantially reduced hexasymmetries (Figure 4, Figure 5).

claims.claim: Firing-rate adaptation can result in hexadirectional modulation.
claims.source: Firing-rate adaptation can result in hexadirectional modulation, but the available cellular data is insufficient to clearly support or refute this option.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated through simulations in Figure 3, showing that repetition suppression can produce hexadirectional modulation under certain conditions.

claims.claim: The available cellular data is insufficient to clearly support or refute the firing-rate adaptation hypothesis.
claims.source: Firing-rate adaptation can result in hexadirectional modulation, but the available cellular data is insufficient to clearly support or refute this option.
claims.evidence: This is an assessment of the current state of empirical evidence regarding adaptation parameters in grid cells.

claims.claim: The magnitude of hexadirectional modulation depends considerably on the subject's navigation pattern.
claims.source: The magnitude of hexadirectional modulation furthermore depends considerably on the subject's navigation pattern, indicating that future fMRI studies could be designed to test which hypothesis most likely accounts for the fMRI measure of grid cells.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated through simulations comparing star-like walks, piecewise linear walks, and random walks across all three hypotheses (Figures 2-5).

claims.claim: Place cells were discovered by O'Keefe and Dostrovsky in 1971.
claims.source: The neural basis of spatial navigation comprises multiple specialized cell types such as place cells (O'Keefe and Dostrovsky, 1971), head-direction (HD) cells (Taube et al., 1990), and grid cells (Hafting et al., 2005), whose activity profiles result from intricate mechanisms of microcircuits in the medial temporal lobes (Tukker et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This is a historical fact supported by the citation to the original discovery paper.

claims.claim: Head-direction cells were discovered by Taube et al. in 1990.
claims.source: The neural basis of spatial navigation comprises multiple specialized cell types such as place cells (O'Keefe and Dostrovsky, 1971), head-direction (HD) cells (Taube et al., 1990), and grid cells (Hafting et al., 2005), whose activity profiles result from intricate mechanisms of microcircuits in the medial temporal lobes (Tukker et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This is a historical fact supported by the citation to the original discovery paper.

claims.claim: Grid cells were discovered by Hafting et al. in 2005.
claims.source: The neural basis of spatial navigation comprises multiple specialized cell types such as place cells (O'Keefe and Dostrovsky, 1971), head-direction (HD) cells (Taube et al., 1990), and grid cells (Hafting et al., 2005), whose activity profiles result from intricate mechanisms of microcircuits in the medial temporal lobes (Tukker et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This is a historical fact supported by the citation to the original discovery paper.

claims.claim: Grid cells activate whenever an animal or human traverses the vertices of a triangular grid tiling the entire environment into equilateral triangles.
claims.source: Grid cells are neurons that activate whenever an animal or human traverses the vertices of a triangular grid tiling the entire environment into equilateral triangles (Hafting et al., 2005; Jacobs et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is a fundamental property of grid cells supported by citations to empirical studies in both animals and humans.

claims.claim: Grid cells may allow the navigating organism to perform vector computations.
claims.source: Grid cells may allow the navigating organism to perform vector computations and may thus constitute an essential neural substrate for different types of spatial navigation including path integration, though their exact functional role still remains unclear (Stemmler et al., 2015; Bush et al., 2015; Moser et al., 2017; Stangl et al., 2018; Gil et al., 2018; Banino et al., 2018; Bierbrauer et al., 2020; Ginosar et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical proposal about grid cell function supported by multiple citations, though the authors note the exact role remains unclear.

claims.claim: The exact functional role of grid cells still remains unclear.
claims.source: Grid cells may allow the navigating organism to perform vector computations and may thus constitute an essential neural substrate for different types of spatial navigation including path integration, though their exact functional role still remains unclear (Stemmler et al., 2015; Bush et al., 2015; Moser et al., 2017; Stangl et al., 2018; Gil et al., 2018; Banino et al., 2018; Bierbrauer et al., 2020; Ginosar et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: This acknowledges the current state of uncertainty in the field despite multiple studies.

claims.claim: In rodents, grid cells can be recorded using electrodes inserted into the medial entorhinal cortex.
claims.source: In rodents, grid cells can be recorded using electrodes inserted into the medial entorhinal cortex (EC).
claims.evidence: This is a standard methodological approach in rodent neuroscience, representing established knowledge.

claims.claim: In humans, measuring grid cells using invasive methods is only rarely possible, e.g., by recording single-neuron activity in epilepsy patients who are neurosurgically implanted with intracranial depth electrodes.
claims.source: In humans, measuring grid cells using invasive methods is only rarely possible, e.g., by recording single-neuron activity in epilepsy patients who are neurosurgically implanted with intracranial depth electrodes (Jacobs et al., 2013; Nadasdy et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This describes the practical and ethical limitations of invasive recordings in humans, supported by citations to rare human studies.

claims.claim: A functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) method has been developed that tests for a hexadirectional modulation of the blood-oxygen-level-dependent signal as a function of the subject's movement direction through a virtual environment.
claims.source: Hence, to enable the detection of grid cells in healthy humans, a functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) method has been developed that tests for a hexadirectional modulation of the blood-oxygen-level-dependent signal as a function of the subject's movement direction through a virtual environment (Doeller et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This describes a methodological innovation supported by citation to the original study.

claims.claim: The phenomenon of hexadirectional modulation of the fMRI signal has been replicated repeatedly in recent years.
claims.source: We here refer to this phenomenon of a hexadirectional modulation of the fMRI signal as 'macroscopic grid-like representations', which has been replicated repeatedly in recent years (e.g. Kunz et al., 2015; Bellmund et al., 2016; Horner et al., 2016; Constantinescu et al., 2016; Bierbrauer et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple replication studies.

claims.claim: The mechanisms underlying the emergence of macroscopic grid-like representations remain still unclear.
claims.source: The mechanisms underlying the emergence of such macroscopic grid-like representations remain still unclear, however.
claims.evidence: This identifies the knowledge gap that motivates the current study.

claims.claim: Three main hypotheses have been developed to explain macroscopic grid-like representations: (i) the 'conjunctive grid by HD cell hypothesis'; (ii) the 'repetition suppression hypothesis'; and (iii) the 'structure-function mapping hypothesis'.
claims.source: Three main hypotheses have been developed: (i) the 'conjunctive grid by HD cell hypothesis'; (ii) the 'repetition suppression hypothesis'; and (iii) the 'structure-function mapping hypothesis' (Figure 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous theoretical work (Doeller et al., 2010; Kunz et al., 2019) and illustrated in Figure 1.

claims.claim: Conjunctive grid by head-direction cells were found in the deeper layers of the entorhinal cortex and in pre- and parasubiculum.
claims.source: The conjunctive grid by HD cell hypothesis rests on two key findings: first, the existence of conjunctive grid by HD cells, which were found in the deeper layers of the entorhinal cortex and in pre- and parasubiculum (Sargolini et al., 2006); second, the observation that the directional tuning of grid cells within the entorhinal cortex is aligned with the grid axes (Doeller et al., 2010), though further studies are needed to corroborate this observation.
claims.evidence: This is an empirical finding supported by citation to the original study.

claims.claim: The directional tuning of grid cells within the entorhinal cortex is aligned with the grid axes.
claims.source: The conjunctive grid by HD cell hypothesis rests on two key findings: first, the existence of conjunctive grid by HD cells, which were found in the deeper layers of the entorhinal cortex and in pre- and parasubiculum (Sargolini et al., 2006); second, the observation that the directional tuning of grid cells within the entorhinal cortex is aligned with the grid axes (Doeller et al., 2010), though further studies are needed to corroborate this observation.
claims.evidence: This is an empirical observation supported by citation, though the authors note it needs further corroboration.

claims.claim: Further studies are needed to corroborate the observation that directional tuning of grid cells is aligned with the grid axes.
claims.source: The conjunctive grid by HD cell hypothesis rests on two key findings: first, the existence of conjunctive grid by HD cells, which were found in the deeper layers of the entorhinal cortex and in pre- and parasubiculum (Sargolini et al., 2006); second, the observation that the directional tuning of grid cells within the entorhinal cortex is aligned with the grid axes (Doeller et al., 2010), though further studies are needed to corroborate this observation.
claims.evidence: This is an assessment of the current state of evidence and a call for future research.

claims.claim: Movements aligned with the grid axes result in increased spiking activity of the conjunctive grid by HD cell population compared to misaligned movements, assuming the directional tuning width is not too broad.
claims.source: Assuming that the directional tuning width of these conjunctive grid by HD cells is not too broad, movements aligned with the grid axes (as compared to misaligned movements) result in increased spiking activity of the conjunctive grid by HD cell population.
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical prediction based on the properties of conjunctive cells, which is tested in the simulations (Figure 2).

claims.claim: The systematic difference in the firing of conjunctive grid by HD cells when moving aligned versus misaligned with the grid axes may cause a macroscopically visible fMRI signal with hexadirectional modulation, given some correlation between population spiking activity and the fMRI signal.
claims.source: Given some correlation between population spiking activity and the fMRI signal, this systematic difference in the firing of conjunctive grid by HD cells when moving aligned versus misaligned with the grid axes may thus cause a macroscopically visible fMRI signal with hexadirectional modulation (Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical prediction illustrated in Figure 1B and tested through simulations.

claims.claim: The conjunctive grid by HD cell hypothesis does not necessarily depend on an alignment between the preferred head directions with the grid axes.
claims.source: We note that the conjunctive grid by HD cell hypothesis does not necessarily depend on an alignment between the preferred head directions with the grid axes.
claims.evidence: This is a clarification about the theoretical requirements of the hypothesis.

claims.claim: The repetition suppression hypothesis is based on the assumption that the phenomenon of repetition suppression also applies to grid cells.
claims.source: The repetition suppression hypothesis (Figure 1C) is based on the assumption that the phenomenon of repetition suppression—i.e., neural activity being reduced for repeated stimuli (Grill-Spector et al., 2006)—also applies to grid cells (Doeller et al., 2010; Killian et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on repetition suppression in general and its potential application to grid cells.

claims.claim: Relatively fewer different grid cells are activated more often during movements aligned with the grid axes, and relatively more different grid cells are activated less often during misaligned movements.
claims.source: Critical to this hypothesis is that relatively fewer different grid cells are activated more often during movements aligned with the grid axes, and relatively more different grid cells are activated less often during misaligned movements.
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical prediction about grid cell activation patterns that is illustrated in Figure 1C and tested in simulations (Figure 3).

claims.claim: A higher degree of repetition suppression at the level of spiking activity or the fMRI signal during aligned movements as compared with misaligned movements can emerge due to systematic differences in how many grid cells are activated how often, resulting in a hexadirectional modulation of fMRI activity.
claims.source: Due to this systematic difference in how many grid cells are activated how often, a higher degree of repetition suppression at the level of spiking activity or the fMRI signal (i.e. fMRI adaptation) during aligned movements as compared with misaligned movements can emerge, again resulting in a hexadirectional modulation of fMRI activity as a function of the subject's movement direction through the spatial environment.
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical prediction tested through simulations in Figure 3.

claims.claim: Studies in rodents have demonstrated that the firing fields of anatomically adjacent grid cells have similar spacing and orientation.
claims.source: Regarding the structure-function mapping hypothesis (Figure 1D), studies in rodents have demonstrated that the firing fields of anatomically adjacent grid cells do not only have similar spacing and orientation (Stensola et al., 2012), but also a similar grid phase offset to a reference location (Heys et al., 2014; Gu et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is an empirical finding supported by citations to rodent studies.

claims.claim: The firing fields of anatomically adjacent grid cells have a similar grid phase offset to a reference location.
claims.source: Regarding the structure-function mapping hypothesis (Figure 1D), studies in rodents have demonstrated that the firing fields of anatomically adjacent grid cells do not only have similar spacing and orientation (Stensola et al., 2012), but also a similar grid phase offset to a reference location (Heys et al., 2014; Gu et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is an empirical finding supported by citations to rodent studies.

claims.claim: Grid cells cluster anatomically.
claims.source: Studies in rodents observed that grid cells also cluster anatomically (Obenhaus et al., 2022; Naumann et al., 2018), which may lead to stronger grid-like representations in some voxels (with an increased percentage of grid cells) than in others (with a decreased percentage of grid cells).
claims.evidence: This is an empirical finding supported by citations to rodent studies.

claims.claim: Anatomical clustering of grid cells may lead to stronger grid-like representations in some voxels than in others.
claims.source: Studies in rodents observed that grid cells also cluster anatomically (Obenhaus et al., 2022; Naumann et al., 2018), which may lead to stronger grid-like representations in some voxels (with an increased percentage of grid cells) than in others (with a decreased percentage of grid cells).
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical inference from the empirical finding of anatomical clustering.

claims.claim: Recordings from a small area of the EC may sample grid cells with similar firing fields, which might show higher average firing rates during aligned movements versus misaligned movements.
claims.source: Therefore, recordings from a small area of the EC (e.g. a sufficiently small voxel of an fMRI scan) may sample grid cells with similar firing fields, which basically behave similarly. It has been suggested that such a grid cell population might show higher average firing rates during aligned movements (because more firing fields are traversed) versus misaligned movements, again resulting in macroscopically visible grid-like representations (Kunz et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical prediction supported by citation and tested in simulations (Figure 4).

claims.claim: All three hypotheses can result in macroscopic grid-like representations under ideal and specific conditions.
claims.source: Our results show that all three hypotheses can result in macroscopic grid-like representations under ideal and specific conditions, but that the strength of the hexadirectional modulation varies by orders of magnitude.
claims.evidence: This is a key finding from the simulations presented in Figures 2-5.

claims.claim: The strength of the hexadirectional modulation varies by orders of magnitude across the three hypotheses.
claims.source: Our results show that all three hypotheses can result in macroscopic grid-like representations under ideal and specific conditions, but that the strength of the hexadirectional modulation varies by orders of magnitude.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5, which compares hexasymmetry values across hypotheses.

claims.claim: The subjects' type of navigation paths through the spatial environments and the exact biological characteristics of grid cells determine to what extent a given hypothesis can explain a hexadirectional population signal in the EC.
claims.source: Key findings are also that the subjects' type of navigation paths through the spatial environments and the exact biological characteristics of grid cells determine to what extent a given hypothesis can explain a hexadirectional population signal in the EC.
claims.evidence: This is a key conclusion from the simulations comparing different trajectory types and parameter values (Figures 2-5).

claims.claim: Star-like walks ensured that the navigation trajectory itself exhibited a hexasymmetry that was essentially zero.
claims.source: During each path segment of star-like walks, the simulated agent started from the same (x/y)-coordinate and navigated along 1 of 360 predefined allocentric navigation directions (0° to 359° in steps of 1°; Figure 2B, left). This ensured that the navigation trajectory itself exhibited a hexasymmetry that was essentially zero.
claims.evidence: This is a property of the star-like walk design, demonstrated in the simulations (Figure 2B).

claims.claim: Each path segment in star-like walks had a length of 300 cm, which was 10 times the grid scale.
claims.source: Each path had a length of 300 cm, which was 10 times the grid scale (see Table 1 for a summary of all model parameters).
claims.evidence: This is a parameter choice documented in Table 1.

claims.claim: For star-like walks, after each path segment was traversed, the agent was 'teleported' back to the initial (x/y)-coordinate and completed the next path segment.
claims.source: After each path segment was traversed, the agent was 'teleported' back to the initial (x/y)-coordinate and completed the next path segment.
claims.evidence: This describes the simulation procedure for star-like walks.

claims.claim: Star-like navigation including teleportation is unusual for real-world experiments but can be implemented in virtual-reality experiments.
claims.source: For real-world experiments, this type of navigation including teleportation is unusual, but it can be implemented in virtual-reality experiments (Vass et al., 2016; Deuker et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to studies that have used teleportation in virtual reality.

claims.claim: Piecewise linear walks consisted of 360 path segments of 300 cm length along the same 360 predefined allocentric navigation directions as in star-like walks, but the path segments were 'unwrapped' such that the starting location of a path segment was identical with the end location of the preceding path segment.
claims.source: During piecewise linear walks, the subject also completed 360 path segments of 300 cm length along the same 360 predefined allocentric navigation directions, as in the star-like walks. In this case, however, the path segments were 'unwrapped' such that the starting location of a path segment was identical with the end location of the preceding path segment (Figure 2C, left).
claims.evidence: This describes the simulation procedure for piecewise linear walks, illustrated in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: The sequence of allocentric navigation directions in piecewise linear walks was randomly chosen.
claims.source: The sequence of allocentric navigation directions was randomly chosen.
claims.evidence: This describes a parameter of the piecewise linear walk simulation.

claims.claim: Piecewise linear walks do not exhibit hexasymmetry a priori.
claims.source: As for star-like walks, piecewise linear walks do not exhibit hexasymmetry a priori.
claims.evidence: This is a property of the piecewise linear walk design by construction.

claims.claim: Random walks were modeled following Kropff and Treves, 2008; Si et al., 2012; D'Albis and Kempter, 2017, which allowed variation of the tortuosity of the paths.
claims.source: For random walks, we modeled navigation trajectories following Kropff and Treves, 2008; Si et al., 2012; D'Albis and Kempter, 2017 (for details, see Methods around Equation 1), which allowed us to vary the tortuosity of the paths.
claims.evidence: This describes the modeling approach for random walks, supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: Tortuosity describes how convoluted a navigation path is, with higher tortuosity meaning more convoluted paths.
claims.source: Tortuosity describes how convoluted a navigation path is (the higher the tortuosity, the more convoluted the path).
claims.evidence: This is a definition of the tortuosity parameter.

claims.claim: Random walks in finite enclosures (circles and squares) with different sizes and orientations had a negligible effect on path hexasymmetry.
claims.source: Apart from random walks in basically infinite environments, we also simulated random walks in finite enclosures (circles and squares) with different sizes and orientations; we found that these restrictions had a negligible effect on path hexasymmetry (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C and Figure 1—figure supplement 3C; for a definition of path hexasymmetry, see the paragraph after the next one).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from simulations shown in supplementary figures.

claims.claim: Random walks exhibit varying degrees of path hexasymmetry because the allocentric navigation directions are not predefined.
claims.source: Because the allocentric navigation directions are not predefined for random walks, they exhibit varying degrees of path hexasymmetry.
claims.evidence: This is a logical consequence of the random walk design.

claims.claim: The longer the simulated random walks, the smaller the path hexasymmetry.
claims.source: The longer the simulated random walks, the smaller the path hexasymmetry (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 4 and derived analytically.

claims.claim: The emergence of grid-like representations based on the conjunctive hypothesis is robust against the specific type of navigation strategy.
claims.source: As we describe below, the emergence of grid-like representations based on the conjunctive hypothesis is robust against the specific type of navigation strategy, whereas the other two hypotheses are sensitive to particular navigation strategies.
claims.evidence: This is a key finding from comparing the three hypotheses across different trajectory types (Figure 5).

claims.claim: The repetition suppression and structure-function mapping hypotheses are sensitive to particular navigation strategies.
claims.source: As we describe below, the emergence of grid-like representations based on the conjunctive hypothesis is robust against the specific type of navigation strategy, whereas the other two hypotheses are sensitive to particular navigation strategies.
claims.evidence: This is a key finding from comparing the three hypotheses across different trajectory types (Figures 3-5).

claims.claim: Future studies on hexadirectional signals should consider the kind of navigation paths subjects will use during a given task.
claims.source: Future studies on hexadirectional signals should thus consider the kind of navigation paths subjects will use during a given task.
claims.evidence: This is a recommendation based on the finding that navigation type affects hexasymmetry.

claims.claim: Conjunctive grid by HD cells with ideal values for HD tuning preciseness and alignment to grid axes resulted in clear hexadirectional modulation of sum grid-cell activity.
claims.source: By modulating the activity of individual grid cells with an HD tuning term aligned with the grid axes (Methods, Equation 3), our simulations indeed showed that these properties resulted in a clear hexadirectional modulation of sum grid-cell activity (Figure 2B–D).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from simulations shown in Figure 2B-D.

claims.claim: Different types of navigation trajectories (star-like, piecewise linear, random) led to similar distributions of sum grid-cell activity as a function of movement direction and similar hexasymmetry values for the conjunctive hypothesis.
claims.source: When considering different types of navigation trajectories, we found that they led to similar distributions of sum grid-cell activity as a function of movement direction and, accordingly, to similar hexasymmetry values (Figure 2B–D).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from simulations comparing trajectory types, shown in Figure 2B-D.

claims.claim: For the conjunctive hypothesis, the directions of maximal activity were aligned with the grid axes.
claims.source: In all three cases, the directions of maximal activity were aligned with the grid axes.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from simulations of the conjunctive hypothesis (Figure 2).

claims.claim: The repetition suppression hypothesis proposes that grid-cell activity is subject to firing-rate adaptation, leading to reduced grid-cell activity when moving along the grid axes compared to other directions.
claims.source: Next, we performed simulations to understand whether the repetition suppression hypothesis (Doeller et al., 2010) results in a hexadirectional modulation of population grid-cell activity. This hypothesis proposes that grid-cell activity is subject to firing-rate adaptation and thus leads to reduced grid-cell activity when moving along the grid axes as compared to when moving along other directions than the grid axes (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This describes the repetition suppression hypothesis, supported by citation and illustrated in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: When moving along the grid axes, the grid fields of fewer grid cells are traversed relatively more often (strong repetition suppression), whereas when moving not along the grid axes, the grid fields of more grid cells are traversed relatively less often (weak repetition suppression).
claims.source: This difference is due to the fact that when the subject moves along the grid axes the grid fields of fewer grid cells are traversed relatively more often (strong repetition suppression), whereas when moving not along the grid axes the grid fields of more grid cells are traversed relatively less often (weak repetition suppression) (Doeller et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This explains the mechanism of the repetition suppression hypothesis, supported by citation.

claims.claim: Star-like and piecewise linear walks resulted in clear and significant hexasymmetry values for the repetition suppression hypothesis.
claims.source: When examining how the different types of navigation trajectories affected hexadirectional modulations based on repetition suppression, we found that star-like and piecewise linear walks resulted in clear and significant hexasymmetry values (Figure 3C and D), which is driven by the long linear segments in these trajectory types.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from simulations shown in Figure 3C and D.

claims.claim: The 30° shift in apparent preferred grid orientation for the repetition suppression hypothesis is due to the adaptation mechanism suppressing grid-cell activity more strongly when moving aligned with a grid axis compared to when moving misaligned.
claims.source: This is due to the fact that the adaptation mechanism suppresses grid-cell activity more strongly when moving aligned with a grid axis as compared to when moving misaligned with a grid axis (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This explains the mechanism behind the 30° shift, illustrated in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: The pattern of sharp peaks at multiples of 60° for the structure-function mapping hypothesis is clearly distinct from the more sinusoidal modulation resulting from the conjunctive hypothesis and the more full-wave rectified sinusoidal modulation resulting from the repetition suppression hypothesis.
claims.source: This pattern is clearly distinct from the more sinusoidal modulation of sum grid-cell activity resulting from the conjunctive grid by HD cell hypothesis (Figure 2) and the more full-wave rectified sinusoidal modulation resulting from the repetition suppression hypothesis (Figure 3).
claims.evidence: This is a comparison of patterns across hypotheses, based on simulations in Figures 2-4.

claims.claim: For the structure-function mapping hypothesis with piecewise linear walks and random walks, hexasymmetry appeared to be considerably lower compared to simulations with star-like walks.
claims.source: When examining the structure-function mapping hypothesis for piecewise linear walks and random walks, hexasymmetry appeared to be considerably lower as compared to simulations with star-like walks (Figure 4B and C).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from simulations shown in Figure 4B and C.

claims.claim: For the structure-function mapping hypothesis with piecewise linear walks and random walks, hexasymmetry values did not show a systematic dependency on the starting location of the subject's navigation trajectory relative to the locations of the grid fields.
claims.source: For both piecewise linear walks and random walks, the hexasymmetry values did not show a systematic dependency on the starting location of the subject's navigation trajectory relative to the locations of the grid fields (Figure 4E and F, left), which is due to the fact that these navigation trajectories randomize the starting locations of all path segments.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from simulations shown in Figure 4E and F, with an explanation of the mechanism.

claims.claim: For the structure-function mapping hypothesis with piecewise linear walks and random walks, the apparent preferred grid orientations varied randomly as a function of the starting location of the very first path segment and did not exhibit systematic shifts.
claims.source: Accordingly, the apparent preferred grid orientations varied randomly as a function of the starting location of the very first path segment and did not exhibit systematic shifts (Figure 4E and F, right), which is in contrast to the clear shifts in the apparent preferred grid orientations for star-like walks (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from simulations shown in Figure 4E and F, compared to Figure 4D.

claims.claim: More realistic clustering concentration parameters resulted in substantially reduced hexasymmetries for the structure-function mapping hypothesis.
claims.source: Accordingly, we found that these more 'realistic' clustering concentration parameters resulted in substantially reduced hexasymmetries for the structure-function mapping hypothesis (described in the next section and in Figure 5).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from simulations shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: The neuronal hexasymmetries for realistic clustering parameters were much lower than those for the realistic conjunctive grid by HD cell hypothesis and for the realistic repetition suppression hypothesis.
claims.source: Furthermore, the neuronal hexaysymmetries were much lower than the ones for the 'realistic' conjunctive grid by HD cell hypothesis and for the 'realistic' repetition suppression hypothesis.
claims.evidence: This is a comparison of hexasymmetry values across hypotheses, shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: For piecewise linear walks in the structure-function mapping hypothesis, subsamples of path segments necessarily exhibit higher path hexasymmetries than the full set of path segments that has zero path hexasymmetry.
claims.source: These subsamples of path segments necessarily exhibit higher path hexasymmetries than the full set of path segments that has zero path hexasymmetry.
claims.evidence: This is a logical consequence of subsampling from a set with zero hexasymmetry.

claims.claim: For piecewise linear walks in the structure-function mapping hypothesis, hexasymmetry values were driven by a subsampling of the movement directions due to the sparsity of the grid-field locations.
claims.source: We thus conclude that, for piecewise linear walks, hexasymmetry values were driven by a subsampling of the movement directions due to the sparsity of the grid-field locations.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion from the analysis of piecewise linear walks in the structure-function mapping hypothesis.

claims.claim: The structure-function mapping hypothesis with very strong (ideal) clustering produces neural hexasymmetry values that are larger than expected from path hexasymmetries only with respect to star-like walks.
claims.source: Taken together, the structure-function mapping hypothesis with very strong ('ideal') clustering produces neural hexasymmetry values that are larger than expected from path hexasymmetries only with respect to star-like walks, including a strong dependence on the subject's starting location (Figure 4D, left).
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion from simulations shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: The range of hexasymmetry values for the structure-function mapping hypothesis with ideal clustering is comparable to those of the repetition suppression hypothesis with ideal parameters.
claims.source: This range of hexasymmetry values is comparable to those of the repetition suppression hypothesis with 'ideal' parameters (Figure 3), but values are at least an order of magnitude smaller than in the 'ideal' conjunctive grid by HD cell case (Figure 2).
claims.evidence: This is a comparison of hexasymmetry values across hypotheses, based on Figures 2-4.

claims.claim: Hexasymmetry values for the structure-function mapping hypothesis with ideal clustering are at least an order of magnitude smaller than in the ideal conjunctive grid by HD cell case.
claims.source: This range of hexasymmetry values is comparable to those of the repetition suppression hypothesis with 'ideal' parameters (Figure 3), but values are at least an order of magnitude smaller than in the 'ideal' conjunctive grid by HD cell case (Figure 2).
claims.evidence: This is a comparison of hexasymmetry values across hypotheses, based on Figures 2-4.

claims.claim: When using realistic clustering concentration parameters, neural hexasymmetry values are further reduced compared to simulations with ideal clustering for the structure-function mapping hypothesis.
claims.source: When using realistic clustering concentration parameters, neural hexasymmetry values are further reduced as compared to simulations with ideal clustering (Figure 5).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from simulations shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: For the conjunctive hypothesis, all three types of navigation led to significant neural hexasymmetries for both ideal and more realistic parameters.
claims.source: For the conjunctive hypothesis, we found that all three types of navigation led to significant neural hexasymmetries. This was the case for both ideal parameters (Mann-Whitney U tests, all U=0, all p<0.001) and for more realistic parameters (Mann-Whitney U tests, all U=0, all p<0.001).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from statistical tests on simulation results shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: For the repetition suppression hypothesis, star-like walks and piecewise linear walks resulted in significant neural hexasymmetries for both ideal and weaker parameters.
claims.source: For the repetition suppression hypothesis, we found that star-like walks and piecewise linear walks resulted in significant neural hexasymmetries for both ideal and weaker parameters (Mann-Whitney U tests, all U=0, all p<0.001), whereas random walks did not (Mann-Whitney U tests, both U>1753, both p>0.405).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from statistical tests on simulation results shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: For the repetition suppression hypothesis, random walks did not result in significant neural hexasymmetries.

claims.claim: For the structure-function mapping hypothesis, most hypothesis conditions resulted in significant neural hexasymmetries compared to path hexasymmetries for both ideal and more realistic parameters, except for random walks with more realistic parameters.
claims.source: Regarding the structure-function mapping hypothesis, the statistical tests showed that most of the hypothesis conditions resulted in significant neural hexasymmetries as compared to the path hexasymmetries multiplied with the average population activities. This was the case for both ideal parameters (Mann-Whitney U tests, all U<736, all p<0.001) and more realistic parameters (Mann-Whitney U tests for star-like walks and piecewise linear walks, all U=0, all p<0.001). Only the hypothesis condition with random walks and more realistic parameters exhibited no significant neural hexasymmetries (Mann-Whitney U test, U=1786, p=0.472).

claims.claim: The results regarding the structure-function mapping hypothesis should be treated with great caution because the neural hexasymmetries for star-like walks heavily depend on the starting location and different starting locations lead to different apparent grid orientations.

First, the neural hexasymmetries for star-like walks heavily depend on the starting location of the subject relative to the grid fields, and different starting locations lead to different apparent grid orientations (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: This is a cautionary note based on findings shown in Figure 4D.

results.result: The manuscript provides background on grid cells, place cells, and head-direction cells as established components of the spatial navigation system, noting that direct recordings of grid cells from humans are rare due to practical limitations.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C10-C17 represent well-established scientific knowledge supported by appropriate citations to foundational studies (O'Keefe and Dostrovsky 1971; Taube et al. 1990; Hafting et al. 2005; Jacobs et al. 2013). These are background claims that accurately reflect the current state of knowledge in the field.

results.result: The manuscript establishes that fMRI studies have developed an indirect measure of grid-cell activity through hexadirectional modulation, which has been replicated, but the underlying mechanisms remain unclear.
results.evaluation: Claims C2-C4, C18-C20 accurately describe the development and replication of fMRI methods for detecting grid cells (Doeller et al. 2010; Kunz et al. 2015; Bellmund et al. 2016) and correctly identify the knowledge gap regarding mechanisms, which motivates the current study.

results.result: Three hypotheses are proposed to explain macroscopic grid-like representations: conjunctive grid by HD cell hypothesis, repetition suppression hypothesis, and structure-function mapping hypothesis, each with specific empirical foundations and theoretical predictions.
results.evaluation: Claims C21-C35 accurately describe the three hypotheses with appropriate citations to supporting empirical work (Sargolini et al. 2006; Doeller et al. 2010; Stensola et al. 2012; Heys et al. 2014; Gu et al. 2018; Kunz et al. 2019). The theoretical predictions are logically derived from the empirical observations.

results.result: The study implements three types of navigation trajectories (star-like walks, piecewise linear walks, and random walks) with specific properties regarding path hexasymmetry, with star-like and piecewise linear walks designed to have zero path hexasymmetry and random walks exhibiting path hexasymmetry that decreases with trajectory length.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C52 describe the simulation methodology with clear specifications documented in Table 1 and demonstrated in figures. The properties of each trajectory type (e.g., zero path hexasymmetry for star-like walks C39, decreasing path hexasymmetry with length for random walks C52) are both theoretically derived and empirically demonstrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

results.result: The emergence of grid-like representations based on the conjunctive hypothesis is robust across navigation strategies, while the repetition suppression and structure-function mapping hypotheses are sensitive to navigation type, indicating that navigation patterns significantly influence hexadirectional modulation magnitude.
results.evaluation: Claims C9, C38, C54-C56 represent key findings demonstrated across Figures 2-5. The robustness of the conjunctive hypothesis across trajectory types is shown in Figure 2B-D and Figure 5, while the sensitivity of the other hypotheses is demonstrated in Figures 3-5 with statistical support (Mann-Whitney U tests, p<0.001).

results.result: For the conjunctive grid by HD cell hypothesis with ideal parameters, all three navigation trajectory types (star-like, piecewise linear, random) produce significant hexadirectional modulation with directions of maximal activity aligned with grid axes, and this holds for both ideal and realistic parameters.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C62, C98, C101 are supported by simulations in Figure 2B-D showing clear hexadirectional modulation across trajectory types, with statistical significance confirmed by Mann-Whitney U tests (all U=0, all p<0.001) as reported in Figure 5. The analytical derivations (Equation 40) match numerical results.

results.result: Hexadirectional modulation is best explained by head-direction tuning aligned to grid axes, with all three hypotheses capable of producing macroscopic grid-like representations under ideal conditions but with hexasymmetry strengths varying by orders of magnitude.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C36-C37 represent the main conclusion, supported by comprehensive simulations in Figures 2-5. Figure 5 directly demonstrates the orders of magnitude difference in hexasymmetry values across hypotheses (conjunctive: ~1000 spk/s ideal, repetition suppression: ~10-20 spk/s ideal, structure-function mapping: ~10-60 spk/s ideal with strong clustering).

results.result: The repetition suppression hypothesis produces significant hexadirectional modulation for star-like and piecewise linear walks but not for random walks, with a characteristic 30° shift in apparent preferred grid orientation due to stronger suppression when moving aligned with grid axes.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C66, C69, C73, C99-C100, C102 are supported by simulations in Figure 3 and statistical tests in Figure 5 (Mann-Whitney U tests: star-like and piecewise linear p<0.001, random walks p>0.405). The 30° shift is demonstrated in Figure 3C-D and explained mechanistically in Figure 3A.

results.result: Firing-rate adaptation can result in hexadirectional modulation, but available cellular data is insufficient to clearly support or refute this hypothesis.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C8 are supported by simulations in Figure 3 demonstrating that adaptation can produce hexadirectional modulation, while the text acknowledges the lack of detailed measurements of adaptation parameters (τr and wr) in grid cells, making biological plausibility uncertain.

results.result: Hexadirectional modulation is not clearly supported by phase offset clustering, as realistic clustering parameters (κs≈0.1) result in substantially reduced hexasymmetries compared to ideal clustering (κs=10), with values much lower than the conjunctive and repetition suppression hypotheses.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C79, C81-C82, C86-C87, C94-C97 are supported by random-field simulations in Figure 4G-S showing realistic clustering parameters (κs≈0.014-0.052) are much lower than ideal values (κs=10), and Figure 5 demonstrating substantially reduced hexasymmetries for realistic parameters compared to other hypotheses.

results.result: For the structure-function mapping hypothesis, significant results for piecewise linear and random walks result from inhomogeneous sampling of movement directions rather than true neural hexasymmetries, with true hexasymmetry only occurring for star-like walks.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C93, C103-C109 are supported by analysis in Figure 4T showing hexasymmetry decreases as 1/√M for piecewise linear walks, indicating path hexasymmetry contribution. The authors provide clear reasoning that only star-like walks produce true neural hexasymmetry for this hypothesis, with appropriate cautions about interpreting statistical significance.

results.result: Environment size, shape, and orientation have negligible effects on hexasymmetry strength for random walks, suggesting experiments can use various environment types to investigate hexadirectional modulations.
results.evaluation: Claims C110-C112 are supported by simulations in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and Figure 1—figure supplement 3 showing minimal dependence of hexasymmetry on boundary size (30-180 cm) and rotation angle (0-360°) for circular and square environments.
